name: The Moon
upright: Seeing through disguises: decoys that study intruders, sensors tuned to the known and the strange, tunnels no eavesdropper can read.
reversed: Believing every reply: forged ARP and DNS answers, a sensor nobody watches, and plaintext crossing hostile ground.
vision: A painted moon hangs low, a lamp the guards lit on purpose; it glows for prowlers already on the road but never calls to anyone asleep. A dog howls at faces it knows from wanted posters; a wolf howls at anything that walks strangely, and sometimes at the wind. From the pool a hundred crayfish crawl to the tower door, each knocking once and scuttling off before it opens, until real travelers cannot get in. Between the two towers the path runs inside a sealed glass pipe, each traveler wrapped whole in a dark cloak. A shadow on the path whispers to each tower that it is the other.
decode: The moon lamp lit on purpose → honeypot: a decoy with no real users, so any visitor is suspect. It may entice the willing but must never entrap.
Dog of wanted posters, wolf howling at odd gaits and wind → signature detection catches known attacks; anomaly detection finds new ones, with more false positives.
Crayfish that knock once and never return → SYN flood: half-open handshakes fill the server's connection queue; SYN cookies blunt it.
The path sealed in glass, travelers cloaked whole → IPsec tunnel mode wraps the entire original packet, as gateway VPNs do; transport mode guards only the payload.
The shadow telling each tower it is the other → man-in-the-middle, often by ARP poisoning: forged replies map the attacker's MAC to another host's IP.
facts: An IDS is passive: it detects and alerts. An IPS sits inline and blocks, so an IPS false positive stops legitimate traffic instead of just raising an alarm.
A honeynet links several honeypots; a padded cell quietly moves a detected intruder into a simulated environment; pseudo flaws are fake vulnerabilities planted as bait.
ARP poisoning works only on the local segment; DNS poisoning plants false name-to-address records to send users to fake sites, and DNSSEC counters it by signing records.
trap: The collective still blurs enticement and entrapment. A honeypot that waits for an intruder already intent on attack is legal enticement; inducing someone who would not have attacked is entrapment.
